column1: Considering a Research Position|Two capable students have not applied to a lab. One is already committed to a competition; the other does not know the project's requirements.|Identical behavior can reflect different conditions. The first student may need to compare time commitments; the second needs a clear entry route and task description.|Ask for the expected tasks, supervision, time and prerequisites. Decide whether to apply, try a small activity or defer without treating the outcome as a character judgment.|Research access and training require legitimate supervision. Do not commit to work you cannot safely or responsibly perform.

A Team Project Falls on Two People|A five-person programming team is near its deadline, but only two members have submitted usable work.|Incomplete work may reflect unclear responsibility, unavailable tools, missing skills, illness or avoidance. Identify which condition is present before assigning motives.|Make deliverables and permissions explicit; ask about blockers; document progress; request the instructor's help if inequity persists.|Do not falsify contribution records or publicly shame classmates.

Late-Night Videos in a Shared Room|One roommate needs to sleep; another frequently watches videos aloud after lights-out, and the discussion becomes accusatory.|Shared space requires attention to actual impact, formal housing policies and feasible agreements rather than judgments about personality.|Describe the noise, propose headphones or a quiet period, review the agreement, and use residence services if necessary.|Threats or repeated serious harassment are safety issues, not ordinary bargaining problems.

Requesting a Grade Review|A student suspects an exam question was incorrectly marked and wonders whether a friend should ask the instructor for a favor.|An evaluation dispute requires the current criteria, evidence and the formal review channel. Personal contacts do not grant marking authority.|Check the rubric and deadline, identify the disputed point, submit a factual request, and keep the reply.|Do not seek preferential treatment or expose another student's marks.

A Friend Asks for Fake Attendance|A friend wants you to sign them in for a missed class and says no one will discover it.|Friendship does not change attendance or honesty rules. You can care about someone without making a false record.|Decline the dishonest action; offer class notes; help the friend find the correct leave procedure.|Do not share credentials or misrepresent who attended.

Club Membership Fees Without Accounting|A club collects fees but refuses to explain spending; members who ask are accused of disloyalty.|Budget questions concern shared resources and authorized procedures, not personal hostility. Keep allegations separate from verified evidence.|Review club rules, request financial records, seek oversight from the designated campus office and decide whether to remain.|Never publish unsupported theft accusations or send further payments to unverified accounts.

A Dispute over Research Authorship|Two students made different contributions to data analysis and experimental design and disagree about author order.|Hours worked and academic status are insufficient alone. Institutional and journal authorship rules, documented contributions and accountability matter.|Create factual contribution statements, review the relevant standards, discuss with authorized supervisors and consult research integrity services if unresolved.|Do not conceal research misconduct or trade authorship for silence.

Pressure to Share Live Location|One partner regards continuous location access as proof of trust while the other wants privacy.|An emotional need can be discussed, but it cannot create automatic rights to another person's whereabouts or device.|Explain needs, propose voluntary safety check-ins and respect refusal or withdrawal of consent.|Stalking, threats or coercion require protection and support, not simply better persuasion.

Customer Data on a Personal Laptop|An intern is told to copy customer names and contact details onto a personal computer to work from home.|A legitimate business task may still involve an unauthorized data transfer. Access and security rules apply to interns too.|Check data classification, request a compliant workspace or authorized sample and obtain proper approval before transferring anything.|Do not send confidential data to personal email or cloud storage.

An Upfront Recruitment Deposit|A recruiter promises employment in exchange for a training deposit and asks for identity and bank details.|Time pressure and a convincing chat group are not evidence of legitimacy. Payment and identity requests must be independently verified.|Stop payment; confirm the employer through an official source; contact bank or relevant authorities if information or funds were exposed.|Never share verification codes or trust a second paid recovery service without verification.

False Stories from Anonymous Accounts|An anonymous account spreads a rumor about a student, and friends recommend public retaliation.|A rumor may entail misinformation, privacy harm or a credible threat. A public argument can amplify the incident.|Save essential evidence, assess safety, use platform reporting and appropriate campus channels, and clarify only verified facts when needed.|Blackmail, stalking or immediate threats should be treated as protection matters.

Graduation with an Uncertain Direction|A graduating student has good marks but no fixed career plan and feels pressured to commit to a ten-year strategy.|Graduation alters roles and access to campus services. Uncertainty can be managed with realistic short-term goals and revisable choices.|List transferable work, compare two viable next steps, identify practical support and set a three-month review point.|Prioritize safe housing, income and essential care over an abstract image of success.
